results.title: Nebius's October 1 price increase is now confirmed and live, verified directly against their own pricing page. | Compute Stacker
results.author: Compute Stacker
highlights:
# Nebius's October 1 price increase is now confirmed and live, verified directly against their own pricing page. | Compute Stacker · LinkedIn · 2026-10-01T00:00:00+00:00

**Compute Stacker**.

---

Nebius's October 1 price increase is now confirmed and live, verified directly against their own pricing page.

H100 moved from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour, a 17% increase. H200 rose 20%, from $4.50 to $5.40. B300 climbed 21%, to $9.50. This is Nebius's second rate hike since May, when H100 was priced at $2.95, meaning the chip has risen roughly 53% in five months alone.

What makes this increase notable isn't the newest hardware, it's the oldest. H100 is a full generation behind Nvidia's current Blackwell chips, and it's still getting repriced upward. Rising demand for last-generation silicon usually signals a capacity shortage more clearly than premium pricing on the newest chip does, buyers aren't paying up for the latest thing, they're paying up because nothing is sitting idle, regardless of generation.

The pattern holds beyond Nebius. According to GetDeploying's pricing tracker, the median on-demand H100 across 40 providers sat at $3.42/GPU-hour as of September 28, up 15% year over year. The same tracker puts hyperscaler pricing at roughly 58% above specialized GPU clouds for identical hardware, a gap that's persisted even as the specialized tier itself gets more expensive.

results.title: Cloud Pricing Goes Dynamic — The Without Surprise Blog
results.author: Timothy O’Brien
highlights:
Nebius, OVHcloud, and CoreWeave repriced inside one month, with memory costs and AI demand pushing from below. Agreements shield part of a bill and cannot shield all of it. The market-driven pricing the book's last chapter describes is arriving from the ground up.

Cloud prices are moving again, and the movement looks like a change in the pricing regime rather than a run of one-off adjustments. Between September 17 and October 1, Nebius told customers that on-demand GPU rates would rise roughly 17 to 21 percent and memory-backed capacity about 41 percent, effective October 1. 1 2 OVHcloud unbundled local storage and public IPv4 addresses from its Public Cloud instances on the same date, which moved the price of an identical configuration up 1.4 to 21.9 percent depending on size. 3 CoreWeave announced that it has continued to contract new compute capacity at higher prices, on short terms of roughly three to six months. 4 Under all three announcements sits the same pressure: memory. TrendForce’s September 30 survey projects conventional DRAM contract prices up another 10 to 15 percent in the fourth quarter, after a year of much larger increases, with server DRAM undersupplied into 2027. 5

...

## What changed in the last month

Nebius notified customers on September 17 rather than issuing a press release: new on-demand rates take effect October 1. 1 The increases step up by chip generation, about 17 percent on H100 instances, 20 percent on H200, 19 percent on B200, 21 percent on the newest B300s, with AMD CPU rates up about 25 percent and memory-backed instances up roughly 41 percent, the largest single line in the notice. It was the company’s second increase in roughly three months. 2 The stock market read the notice as pricing power rather than distress: Nebius shares climbed about 10 percent that morning, and operators that had sent no note at all caught a bid alongside it. 6 The detail to notice is the memory line. Providers bundle memory into instance pricing, so it rarely appears on its own on a bill. A 41 percent increase on the memory line says the component inside every instance is repricing, not just the scarce GPUs on top.

OVHcloud did not raise an instance rate at all. What changed on October 1 is what the price includes. Local storage and public IPv4 addresses, previously bundled with Generation 3 instances, became separate billing lines, about €109 per terabyte-month for storage and about €1.97 per month for an address, and the total for an identical configuration rose 1.4 to 21.9 percent: a b3-8 went from €37 to €45 a month, a c3-4 from €33 to €41. 3 The company also replaced its Savings Plans grid, cutting terms to 12 or 36 months at 15 and 30 percent discounts, where the old grid had offered 35 percent on a 12-month commitment. Customers already inside a plan keep their guaranteed compute rate until the end of the commitment, but from October 1 the storage and address lines bill at full price, outside the guarantee.

CoreWeave’s announcement was about the direction of new contracts: since June 30 it has signed new compute capacity at higher prices, and the quarter’s new contracts are short-dated, roughly three to six months, at about $40 million per megawatt on an annualized basis. Contracted power rose from about 3.7 gigawatts at June 30 to about 4.2 gigawatts by August 11. 4 Customers with billions in new commitments are signing short. When a seller offers shorter terms at higher prices, the market is saying that the length of the agreement, the certainty, is itself a product whose price went up.

...

1. Yahoo Finance, September 17, 2026: Nebius Group (NBIS) Raises AI Cloud Prices As Compute Demand Tests Customer Costs — customer communication rather than a public release; higher on-demand rates effective October 1, 2026; compute demand as the stated driver.

3. Octave Klaba, OVHcloud blog, October 1, 2026: Public Cloud: Pricing changes as of October 1, 2026 — identical configurations up 1.4 to 21.9 percent; hourly instance prices unchanged; local storage about €109 per terabyte-month and IPv4 about €1.97 per month as separate lines; b3-8 €37 to €45 and c3-4 €33 to €41 examples; Savings Plans reduced to 12- and 36-month terms at −15 and −30 percent effective September 1, 2026; existing plans guaranteed through the commitment with storage and IPv4 outside the guarantee from October 1.

Tomorrow, AWS will raise GPU capacity block prices for the third time in 2026.

+15% in January. +20% in July. +15% effective tomorrow. That's a cumulative ~35% increase on GPU compute in under a year.

And this is before you factor in the broader picture: AWS's announced $496B backlog means capacity is tightening through 2027-2028. Demand is outpacing supply, and pricing reflects that. And this isn’t unique to AWS, the same dynamics apply across GCP, Azure, and every other compute provider.

results.title: Nebius GPU prices rise across the board, up to… · Slicast
highlights:
Trade press Slicast · October 1, 2026 at 21:01 UTC · Global · Source: KuCoin News

A notable shift is emerging in the AI computing power market: while cloud providers continue to expand their data centers, rental prices for certain high-end GPUs are not declining with increased supply—they continue to rise.

According to a price adjustment notice sent by Nebius to its customers, effective October 1, 2026, the company plans to increase prices for multiple on-demand GPU instances by approximately 17% to 21%. The proposed hourly rates per GPU are: H100 rising from $3.85 to $4.50 (a 16.9% increase), H200 from $4.50 to $5.40 (20% increase), B200 from $7.15 to $8.50 (18.9% increase), and B300 from $7.85 to $9.50 (21% increase).

This price adjustment sends a significant signal: the pace of growth in AI computing demand may still outstrip the rate at which high-end GPUs, power, and data center capacity are coming online. Unlike traditional cloud computing, the core scarce resources for AI cloud services extend beyond servers to include GPU availability, power access, liquid cooling systems, networking equipment, and data centers capable of supporting high-density racks. If any single component encounters a bottleneck, new computing power cannot be rapidly deployed.

At the Goldman Sachs Technology Conference, Nebius management stated that the company's visibility into customer demand has extended from approximately 18 months to over 24 months, with some customers already reserving compute capacity for the first half of 2028. The company previously conducted price testing for scarce Blackwell capacity, achieving transaction prices approximately 15% higher than previous peak prices and roughly 20% higher than standard sales pipeline quotes.

The significance of Nebius's price increase lies not merely in the ability to charge approximately 20% more per GPU hour, but in confirming that supply and demand in the AI computing market still favor suppliers. A primary past market concern was that simultaneous launches of numerous data centers could eventually lead to GPU leasing market oversupply, potentially resulting in lower utilization rates, extended payback periods, and asset impairment for companies built under assumptions of higher prices. Nebius signals the opposite: the company is raising prices not only for new B200 and B300 models but also for H100 and H200, which have been on the market for years. This indicates that demand extends beyond the latest architecture, with previous-generation GPUs still offering sufficient performance and cost efficiency for model fine-tuning, inference, scientific computing, and certain enterprise workloads.

...

However, the on-demand price increase will not uniformly raise all of Nebius's revenue by 20%. Large customers typically sign multi-year contracts with fixed prices, minimum purchase volumes, and service terms that cannot be immediately repriced according to new public rates. This adjustment most directly impacts on-demand and short-term compute contracts rather than long-term capacity agreements already signed by clients like Meta.

results.author: FastGPU
highlights:

Today, October 7, AWS adds an increase of its own to EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML.

Everything below comes from the daily prices FastGPU records across GPU clouds, published as an open dataset, and from AWS's own pricing page. Every figure links to the page it comes from.

## 15 increases, no cuts

## AWS Capacity Blocks: 15% more from today, up to 26.5% outside the US 

AWS's Capacity Blocks pricing page says:

> Effective October 7, 2026, hourly rates per accelerator across all available AWS Regions will be: P6-B300 at $16.146 ($16.819 in AWS GovCloud Regions), P6-B200 at $14.208 ($14.801 in AWS GovCloud Regions), P5en at $7.895, P5e at $6.866, P5 at $5.970, P4de at $2.546, and P4d at $1.696.

Against the rates AWS published before, as recorded in our price-change log, per GPU per hour:

| P4de | A100 80GB | $2.214 | $2.546 | +15.0% |

AWS now charges one rate in every Region, so blocks that used to be cheaper outside the US (P5 and P5en) rise the most. AWS publishes these rates to a tenth of a cent; our log shows them rounded to the cent. AWS also says Capacity Block reservation prices are dynamic and are updated periodically based on supply and demand, and: "All other EC2 Capacity Block prices, as well as prices on fixed pricing models like On-Demand and Savings Plans, remain unchanged."

## What it means if you rent 

- A Capacity Block is reserved capacity: you book a start date and a length, and AWS guarantees the GPUs for it. That is a different product from an on-demand GPU you can stop at any time. Still, for scale: the cheapest posted H100 SXM is $1.79/hr at Vast.ai as of 2026-10-07 01:46 UTC, the September-end median across 16 providers was $3.70/hr, and a P5 Capacity Block is now $5.970/hr.
- If you were planning a reserved block, re-run the numbers: the reserve-or-rent calculator has the October 7 rates, and the GPU cluster page prices N GPUs for M months across providers' published term rates.
- List prices change without notice. A price alert emails you when a GPU drops below a price you choose, with no account.

## Data and method 

Posted prices, not transactions. The September report is computed from the recorded daily prices once the month is over and then frozen; every dated change is in the price-change log, also as JSON at `https://fastgpu.co/api/v1/price-changes`. The daily series is an open dataset (CC BY 4.0). Live prices in this post are as of 2026-10-07 01:46 UTC; the linked pages show the current ones. Some provider links on FastGPU are affiliate links; tables and every "cheapest" figure are ordered strictly by price.

## How much does it cost to rent a GPU?

A GPU rental price pays for access to a configured cloud machine for a period of time. The useful comparison is the cost of completing your workload, including the whole plan, runtime and additional fees. Chip model alone does not identify an equivalent service.

results.title: H100 price per hour, October 2026: 11 clouds compared · ClearCompute
results.author: Ronit Ahuja
highlights:
The short answer

On 5 October 2026, one H100 80GB SXM listed at $2.69 to $12.29 per GPU-hour on-demand across nine clouds, and the Vast.ai marketplace median was $1.80. Five specialist clouds charged between $3.20 and $4.50. The hyperscalers charged $6.88 (AWS), $11.06 (Google Cloud) and $12.29 (Azure), though a three-year commitment brings them down to between $2.97 and $5.40. For an inference server, four things matter as much as the rate: the smallest unit you can rent, egress, billing increments and how fast the price is moving.

## Prices rose this autumn#

- Nebius raised on-demand prices on 1 October: H100 by 17% ($3.85 to $4.50), H200 by 20% and B200 by 19%.

Any price survey goes stale within weeks, this one included. For today's number, live trackers such as gpufinder.dev, which polls 22 vendors every hour, and SkyPilot's GPU Compass are better sources. A survey is more useful for explaining what the number buys.

Are GPU prices going down?

Not this autumn. Nebius raised on-demand prices on 1 October 2026 (H100 from $3.85 to $4.50), AWS announced a 15% rise in Capacity Block prices from 7 October, and Verda's H100 rose from $3.37 to $3.77 between 22 September and 5 October.
